items.stem: Describe Blitzkrieg tactics.
items.answer: Aircraft such as Stuka dive-bombers attacked airfields, roads and defences. Tanks concentrated to break through at a weak point. Motorised infantry followed quickly to hold ground. Forces encircled the enemy rather than attacking head-on. Speed and surprise caused confusion and panic.

items.stem: (a) Describe the Battle of Britain. [4] (b) Why did the RAF win the Battle of Britain? [6]
items.answer: (a) From July 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked shipping and ports in the Channel. In August it attacked RAF airfields and radar stations. The RAF was close to exhaustion by early September. On 7 September the Luftwaffe switched to bombing London. On 15 September heavy German losses showed the RAF was undefeated, and Sea Lion was postponed. (b) Radar gave early warning of German attacks. Spitfires and Hurricanes were effective fighters, and factories replaced losses quickly. The RAF fought over home territory, so shot-down pilots could fly again. The Luftwaffe switched from airfields to London in September. German fighters had limited fuel time over Britain.

items.stem: ‘Blitzkrieg tactics were the main reason for German success in 1939-40.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Concentrated tanks and aircraft broke through and encircled enemy forces. Speed caused panic and collapse in Poland and France. Against: The Allies made mistakes, such as relying on the Maginot Line and moving into Belgium. France's leadership and communications were poor. The Nazi-Soviet Pact meant Germany had no war in the east. Poland was attacked from two sides. Judgement: Blitzkrieg was very effective, but it succeeded because of Allied mistakes and the favourable position created by the Nazi-Soviet Pact.

items.stem: On 22 June 1941 German forces invaded the Soviet Union in Operation Barbarossa. Describe Operation Barbarossa in 1941.
items.answer: It began on 22 June 1941 with over three million Axis troops. Three army groups attacked towards Leningrad, Moscow and Ukraine. items.stem: In July 1943 the largest tank battle in history was fought at Kursk. Describe the Battle of Stalingrad.
items.answer: The German Sixth Army attacked Stalingrad in August 1942. Fierce street fighting took place in the ruined city. In November 1942 Soviet forces encircled the Germans in Operation Uranus. Hitler refused to allow a retreat and attempts to supply the army by air failed. Paulus surrendered in February 1943 and about 91,000 Germans were taken prisoner.

items.stem: In February 1943 the German Sixth Army surrendered at Stalingrad. ‘The Battle of Stalingrad was the turning point of the war on the Eastern Front.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: A whole German army was destroyed or captured. It ended German advances towards the oil fields of the Caucasus. It was a huge boost to Soviet morale and a blow to German prestige. Against: The failure before Moscow in December 1941 ended hopes of a quick victory. Kursk in July 1943 was the last German offensive; after it the Red Army held the initiative. Soviet industrial production and Lend-Lease decided the long war. Judgement: Stalingrad was the decisive psychological and military turning point, though Moscow had already ended Blitzkrieg and Kursk confirmed the shift.

items.answer: It was a surprise attack on Sunday 7 December 1941, without a declaration of war. Over 350 Japanese aircraft took off from six carriers. Eight US battleships were damaged or sunk. items.stem: In August 1945 the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. ‘The atomic bombs were the main reason for Japan's surrender in 1945.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Two cities were destroyed, showing the USA could destroy Japan without invasion. The Emperor referred to a new and most cruel bomb in his surrender broadcast. Against: Japan had already lost its navy and air force and its cities were being destroyed by conventional bombing. The US blockade was starving Japan. The Soviet declaration of war on 8 August ended hopes of Soviet mediation. Island hopping had brought US forces to Japan's doorstep. Judgement: The bombs were the immediate trigger for surrender, but Japan was already defeated; the Soviet declaration of war was also decisive.

items.stem: In June 1942 the US navy won a major victory at Midway. How important was the Battle of Midway in the defeat of Japan? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It destroyed four carriers and ended Japanese expansion. It gave the USA the initiative for the rest of the war. Against: US industrial strength was the underlying reason for victory. Island hopping and submarine warfare wore Japan down. The atomic bombs and Soviet entry ended the war. Judgement: Midway was the turning point, but US industrial superiority explains why Japan could not recover from it.

items.stem: Describe the D-Day landings of 6 June 1944.
items.answer: About 156,000 Allied troops landed on five beaches in Normandy. US troops landed at Utah and Omaha, British at Gold and Sword and Canadians at Juno. Operation Fortitude meant German reserves were held back near Calais.

items.stem: (a) Describe the Allied strategic bombing of Germany. [4] (b) Why did the Allies carry out strategic bombing of Germany? [6]
items.answer: (a) RAF Bomber Command carried out area bombing of cities at night. The USAAF attempted precision bombing of factories by day. The bombing of Hamburg in July 1943 created a firestorm that killed about 40,000 people. From 1944 oil plants and transport were targeted. Dresden was destroyed in February 1945. About 55,000 Bomber Command aircrew were killed. (b) To destroy German war industry and transport. To break the morale of German workers. It was the only way Britain could hit Germany directly before an invasion was possible. To help the USSR by forcing Germany to divert resources to air defence. To weaken the Luftwaffe before D-Day.

items.stem: When Allied troops entered the Nazi camps in 1945 they found evidence of mass murder on an enormous scale. Describe the Nazi persecution and murder of the Jews during the Second World War.
items.answer: Jews in occupied Poland were forced into ghettos such as Warsaw and Lodz. From June 1941 Einsatzgruppen shot hundreds of thousands of Jews in the USSR. The Wannsee Conference in January 1942 coordinated the Final Solution. Death camps such as Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau used gas chambers. About six million Jews were murdered. Roma, disabled people and others were also murdered.

items.stem: ‘D-Day was the most important reason for the defeat of Germany.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It opened the second front that Stalin had demanded. It led to the liberation of France and the advance into Germany from the west. It forced Germany to fight on two major fronts at once. Against: Most German forces were destroyed on the Eastern Front, for example at Stalingrad and Kursk. Strategic bombing damaged German industry and transport. US and Soviet industrial production far exceeded Germany's. Hitler's mistakes, such as the invasion of the USSR. Judgement: D-Day shortened the war, but the Eastern Front destroyed most of the German army, so it was the more important factor.

items.answer: Careful planning and training over two years. Operation Fortitude deceived the Germans about where the landings would be. The Allies had complete air superiority. items.stem: Describe the evacuation from Dunkirk in 1940.
items.answer: British and French troops were trapped around Dunkirk after the German breakthrough. Hitler halted his tanks for several days. Operation Dynamo used naval ships and hundreds of small civilian boats. About 338,000 troops were rescued between 26 May and 4 June. Most heavy equipment was left behind.

items.stem: How important were Hitler's mistakes in the German defeat on the Eastern Front? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: He delayed the attack on Moscow in 1941. He refused to let the Sixth Army break out at Stalingrad. Brutal occupation policies turned potential allies against Germany. Against: Soviet resistance and leadership improved. The size of the USSR and the winter. Soviet industrial strength and Lend-Lease. Judgement: Hitler's mistakes made defeat worse, but Soviet resources and resistance were the main reasons.

items.stem: In August 1945 the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. (a) Why did Japan attack Pearl Harbor? [6] (b) ‘The atomic bombs were the main reason for Japan's surrender in 1945.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) Japan wanted an empire in Asia with raw materials such as oil and rubber. The USA had imposed an oil embargo in 1941 after Japan moved into Indochina. Destroying the US Pacific Fleet would give Japan time to conquer South-East Asia. Japanese leaders hoped the USA would then accept a negotiated peace. (b) For: Two cities were destroyed, showing the USA could destroy Japan without invasion. The Emperor referred to a new and most cruel bomb in his surrender broadcast. Against: Japan had already lost its navy and air force and its cities were being destroyed by conventional bombing. The US blockade was starving Japan. The Soviet declaration of war on 8 August ended hopes of Soviet mediation. Island hopping had brought US forces to Japan's doorstep. Judgement: The bombs were the immediate trigger for surrender, but Japan was already defeated; the Soviet declaration of war was also decisive.

items.stem: Describe the Nazi persecution and murder of the Jews during the Second World War.
items.answer: Jews in occupied Poland were forced into ghettos such as Warsaw and Lodz. From June 1941 Einsatzgruppen shot hundreds of thousands of Jews in the USSR. The Wannsee Conference in January 1942 coordinated the Final Solution. Death camps such as Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau used gas chambers. About six million Jews were murdered. Roma, disabled people and others were also murdered.

items.stem: How far did strategic bombing contribute to the Allied victory in Europe? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It forced Germany to divert fighters, guns and men to air defence. Attacks on oil and transport in 1944-45 crippled the German war economy. It destroyed much of the Luftwaffe before D-Day. Against: German production rose until late 1944. Civilian morale did not collapse. Losses of aircrew were very high. The war was mainly won on land, especially in the east. Judgement: Bombing was not decisive on its own, but by 1944 it was a major contribution because of the attacks on oil and the diversion of German resources.

items.stem: Source A: a Nazi election poster from 1932 (description). The poster shows a crowd of grim, unemployed men and women with the caption “Our last hope: Hitler”. Source B: an extract from a modern history book (illustrative). “Hitler did not seize power; he was given it. In January 1933 a small group of conservatives around Hindenburg handed him the chancellorship, believing they could tame him.” Explain how a historian investigating how Hitler came to power would use Source A differently from Source B.
items.answer: Source A is primary evidence from the time. Message: It suggests that the unemployed saw Hitler as their only hope during the Depression. It must be evaluated for its purpose: to win votes from Germans suffering in the Depression. Source B is a later interpretation. Argument: It argues Hitler became Chancellor because of a deal by conservative politicians, not because of the Depression alone. The historian should test this argument against evidence such as Source A, and agree with or challenge it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying A as contemporary evidence; 1 mark for identifying B as a later interpretation; up to 2 marks for explaining the different uses (evidence to be evaluated vs argument to be tested) with details [4]

items.stem: Describe the Battle of Britain.
items.answer: From July 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked shipping and ports in the Channel. In August it attacked RAF airfields and radar stations. The RAF was close to exhaustion by early September. On 7 September the Luftwaffe switched to bombing London. On 15 September heavy German losses showed the RAF was undefeated, and Sea Lion was postponed.

items.stem: How central was the persecution and murder of the Jews to the aims of the Nazi regime? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Antisemitism was central to Nazi ideology from the beginning. The killing continued even when it took trains and resources from the war effort. The Final Solution was organised across the whole of occupied Europe. Against: Winning the war and conquering Lebensraum in the east were the regime's main priorities. Policy developed in stages and was radicalised by the war, especially the invasions of Poland and the USSR. The regime also persecuted and murdered other groups, such as Roma and disabled people. Judgement: The murder of the Jews was a central aim of the regime, shown by the resources committed to it even in defeat.

items.answer: Question 1 asks for a judgement about the war in the Pacific, so the answer must weigh factors (for example, the point that it destroyed four carriers and ended Japanese expansion, against the point that US industrial strength was the underlying reason for victory) and reach a conclusion. items.stem: Read the interpretation, an extract from a modern history book (illustrative): “In 1923 the Republic faced invasion, economic collapse and a putsch, yet it survived. That it did so suggests its foundations were stronger than its enemies believed.” (a) What is the interpretation in the extract? [2] (b) Use your own knowledge to explain how far this interpretation is supported by the evidence. [2]
items.answer: (a) It argues the Republic was not doomed because it survived the worst crisis of 1923. (b) Evidence that supports the interpretation: It survived the crises of 1919-23. Evidence that challenges it: It was linked to defeat and the hated Treaty of Versailles. Judgement: The Republic had serious weaknesses from the start, but its survival and recovery in the 1920s show it was not doomed; the Depression was needed to bring it down.
